The Myrrh-Bearing Women at the Tomb

Icons

Scriptural scenes

The Myrrh-Bearing Women at the Tomb

Myrrhbearers · Ointment-bearing Women · Women at the Sepulchre

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

Mark 16:1–8

Luke 24:1–11

Matthew 28:1–10

King James Version · Scripture previews

The published iconographic article explains the women’s name through the ointments they brought to Christ’s tomb. It places their Orthodox commemoration on the second Sunday after Pascha. Their vessels identify the purpose of their visit: care for the body of Jesus.

[1] Opening paragraph

What is depicted

The women approach carrying vessels. An angel in white points toward the empty tomb and burial cloths, announcing that Christ has risen. The article describes this image as a representation of the Gospel encounter, in contrast with the theological Descent into Hades composition.

[1] Opening description; A short history of this iconic representation

History and tradition

The selected Vologda icon is dated by its source to the end of the fifteenth or beginning of the sixteenth century. Its subject is the women’s encounter at the tomb; other images called Myrrhbearers instead assemble the commemorated saints without narrating this scene.

[2] File description and displayed historic reproduction

Published explanation

The article’s discussion of hymnography emphasizes the women’s grief, their encounter with the angel, and their commission to announce the Resurrection. The focus is the empty tomb’s good news, rather than the depiction of Christ emerging from it.

[1] Some of the themes occurring in the texts; The encounter with the angel; Run to tell the disciples

And he saith unto them, Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.

[3] Mark 16:6
